title: ISTQB CTFL v4.0.1 - Hard Mock Exam

questions.question: Error guessing anticipates errors, defects and failures based on the tester's knowledge. Which of the following is NOT a typical source of that knowledge?

options.A: The types of failures that have occurred in other, similar applications
options.B: The equivalence partitions and boundary values derived from the requirements specification
options.C: How the application has worked in the past
options.D: The types of errors developers tend to make, and the defects that result

questions.why_correct: CTFL 4.4.1: error guessing is based on knowledge of how the application has worked in the past, the types of errors developers tend to make and the resulting defects, and the types of failures in other similar applications. Partitions and boundary values derived from a specification belong to black-box techniques (EP, BVA), not experience-based ones.

option_notes.A: Typical source.
option_notes.B: NOT a source - this is black-box test design.
option_notes.C: Typical source.
option_notes.D: Typical source.

questions.distractor_note: B sounds like valuable tester knowledge, but it is systematic specification-based derivation, which belongs to a different technique category.
questions.alt_wording: Which knowledge does error guessing NOT rely on?

questions.question:
Four test cases cover these requirements:
T1: R1, R2, R3, R4
T2: R1, R2, R5
T3: R5, R6
T4: R3, R4, R6

Using ADDITIONAL coverage prioritization, which test case is executed SECOND?

options.A: T4
options.B: T2 or T4, because they tie on coverage
options.C: T2
options.D: T3

questions.why_correct: T1 runs first (highest coverage: 4). Additional coverage after T1: T2 adds R5 (1), T3 adds R5 and R6 (2), T4 adds R6 (1). T3 adds the most new coverage, so it runs second. With T1 + T3, all six requirements are covered.

option_notes.A: T4 adds only R6.
option_notes.B: This is plain coverage-based prioritization (T2 and T4 each cover 3). Additional coverage looks at NEW items only.
option_notes.C: T2 adds only R5.
option_notes.D: Correct.

questions.distractor_note: B is the trap of using total coverage instead of additional coverage after the first pick.
questions.alt_wording: After the highest-coverage test, which test adds the most not-yet-covered items?

questions.question: A production failure in build 4.2.1 cannot be reproduced, because nobody knows which versions of the test scripts, test data and environment configuration were used when that build was tested. Which practice would MOST directly have prevented this?

options.A: Configuration management: identifying, version-controlling and tracking changes to configuration items and recording baselines
options.B: Defect management: logging the failure with severity and priority
options.C: Risk-based testing: testing the riskiest functions first
options.D: The test pyramid: automating more component tests

questions.why_correct: CTFL 5.4: configuration management identifies, controls and tracks work products such as test plans, test cases, test scripts, test data, test environment items and test results as configuration items. It records changes and baselines so that a previous configuration can be restored to reproduce earlier test results, and it keeps traceability throughout the test process.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Defect reporting matters, but it does not keep track of which testware versions were used.
option_notes.C: Changes the order of testing, not the ability to rebuild a configuration.
option_notes.D: About test granularity and automation, not version control.

questions.distractor_note: B is close, because defect management uses defect reports to support reproduction, but the missing information here is about versions, which only CM provides.
questions.alt_wording: Which discipline lets a team restore the exact testware used for an earlier build?

questions.question:
Test cases have these priorities (1 = highest) and dependencies:
TC-A: priority 1, depends on TC-D
TC-B: priority 2
TC-C: priority 3, depends on TC-E
TC-D: priority 5
TC-E: priority 4

Which execution order BEST follows priority while respecting the dependencies?

options.A: TC-D, TC-E, TC-A, TC-B, TC-C
options.B: TC-B, TC-D, TC-A, TC-E, TC-C
options.C: TC-D, TC-A, TC-B, TC-E, TC-C
options.D: TC-A, TC-B, TC-C, TC-E, TC-D

questions.why_correct: CTFL 5.1.5: if a higher-priority test case depends on a lower-priority one, the lower-priority one must run first. TC-A (priority 1) needs TC-D, so TC-D then TC-A. Next highest available is TC-B (2). TC-C (3) needs TC-E (4), so TC-E then TC-C.

option_notes.A: Runs TC-E earlier than needed, delaying the higher-priority TC-A and TC-B.
option_notes.B: Runs TC-B before the dependency chain of the priority-1 test case.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Ignores both dependencies.

questions.distractor_note: A 'front-loads all prerequisites', which respects dependencies but not priority.
questions.alt_wording: How should dependencies change a pure priority order?

questions.question:
A business analyst, given no domain training and a two-day deadline, misreads a VAT regulation and writes a requirement with the wrong tax rate. The developer implements it exactly as written. After release, customers are overcharged.

Which of the following is the ROOT CAUSE?

options.A: Customers being overcharged in production
options.B: The lack of domain training combined with the time pressure
options.C: The analyst's misreading of the regulation
options.D: The requirement containing the wrong tax rate

questions.why_correct: A root cause is the fundamental reason for a problem - a situation that leads to an error. Here the lack of training and time pressure led the analyst to make the error (misreading). The error produced a defect (wrong requirement), which led to a failure (overcharging). Identifying the root cause helps prevent similar defects in future.

option_notes.A: This is the FAILURE observed in operation.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: This is the human ERROR (mistake), caused by the root cause.
option_notes.D: This is the DEFECT in a work product (the requirement).

questions.distractor_note: C vs B is the close pair: the misreading is the error; WHY the analyst misread it (no training, time pressure) is the root cause.
questions.alt_wording: What is the fundamental reason that led to the human mistake in this scenario?

questions.question:
A minimized decision table for a discount has these columns (Y = true, N = false, - = does not matter):

R1: Member=N, Coupon=N, Total>100=-  -> no discount
R2: Member=N, Coupon=Y, Total>100=-  -> 5%
R3: Member=Y, Coupon=-, Total>100=N  -> 5%
R4: Member=Y, Coupon=N, Total>100=Y  -> 10%
R5: Member=Y, Coupon=Y, Total>100=Y  -> 15%

All combinations are feasible. What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% decision table coverage of THIS table?
questions.why_correct: In decision table testing, the coverage items are the columns that contain feasible combinations of conditions. 100% coverage means exercising every column. This minimized table has 5 columns, so at least 5 test cases are needed - one per column. Each '-' column can be covered with any one value of the 'does not matter' condition.

option_notes.A: No two columns can be exercised by one test case; each test case matches exactly one column.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Miscount - expanding only some '-' entries.
option_notes.D: 8 is the number of columns in the FULL (unminimized) table; coverage is measured against the table being used.

questions.distractor_note: D is the key trap: candidates expand the '-' entries back to 2^3 = 8, but coverage is measured against the columns of the given table.
questions.alt_wording: How many coverage items does this minimized decision table contain?

questions.question:
Which of the following are typically TEST IMPLEMENTATION work products?
i. Stubs and service virtualizations
ii. Test execution schedule
iii. Test data requirements
iv. Test logs
v. Test charters

options.A: i and ii
options.B: ii and iii
options.C: i, ii and iv
options.D: iii and v

questions.why_correct: CTFL 1.4.3: test implementation work products include test procedures, manual and automated test scripts, test suites, test data, the test execution schedule, and test environment items such as stubs, drivers, simulators and service virtualizations. Test data REQUIREMENTS and test charters are test design products; test logs are test execution products.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Test data requirements (iii) come from test design; the test data itself comes from implementation.
option_notes.C: Test logs (iv) are produced during test execution.
option_notes.D: Both are test design work products.

questions.distractor_note: iii is the subtle trap: 'test data' is implementation, but 'test data requirements' is design.
questions.alt_wording: Which testware is created or acquired so that tests are ready to execute?

questions.topic: Estimation Based on Ratios From Total Effort
questions.question: Historical data shows a development-to-test effort ratio of 5:2. For a new similar project, the TOTAL effort (development plus testing) is planned at 1,400 person-days. Using estimation based on ratios, what is the test effort?

options.A: 280 person-days
options.B: 400 person-days
options.C: 560 person-days
options.D: 1,000 person-days

questions.why_correct: A ratio of 5:2 means testing is 2 of every 7 parts of total effort. Test effort = 1,400 x 2/7 = 400 person-days (development = 1,000). Check: 1,000 : 400 = 5 : 2.

option_notes.A: 1,400 / 5 - divides by one side of the ratio only.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Applies 2/5 to the TOTAL; that would only be correct if 1,400 were the development effort.
option_notes.D: This is the development effort.

questions.distractor_note: The syllabus example applies the ratio to DEVELOPMENT effort. Here the given figure is TOTAL effort, so 560 is the trap.
questions.alt_wording: If dev:test is 5:2 and the total is 1,400, how much is testing?

questions.topic: Black-Box Test Case Independence From Implementation
questions.question: Which statement about test technique categories is MOST accurate?

options.A: Black-box test cases stay useful when the implementation changes but the required behavior stays the same.
options.B: Experience-based techniques are mainly useful when complete, detailed specifications are available.
options.C: Black-box coverage is measured as the percentage of code executed by the tests.
options.D: White-box techniques are especially good at detecting missing requirements, because they do not depend on the specification.

questions.why_correct: CTFL 4.1: black-box techniques are based on the specified behavior, independent of how the software is implemented, so if the implementation changes but the required behavior stays the same, the test cases are still useful. White-box techniques cannot detect missing requirements (defects of omission). Experience-based techniques help find defects missed by other techniques and are useful when specifications are poor. Black-box coverage is measured against items in the test basis.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Experience-based techniques are especially useful when specifications are poor or missing.
option_notes.C: That describes white-box coverage; black-box coverage is measured against the test basis.
option_notes.D: Reversed: white-box testing cannot reveal requirements that were never implemented.

questions.distractor_note: D sounds logical ('independent of the spec') but white-box tests only exercise code that exists.
questions.alt_wording: Which technique category keeps its test cases valid across refactoring?

questions.question:
User story: 'As a shopper, I want free shipping on domestic orders of $50 or more so that I am encouraged to buy more.' Acceptance criteria: domestic orders of $50.00 or more ship free; domestic orders below $50.00 pay standard shipping; international orders always pay shipping.

Which proposed ATDD test case should NOT be included?

options.A: Domestic order of $50.00 -> free shipping
options.B: International order of $80.00 -> shipping charged
options.C: Domestic order of $49.99 -> standard shipping charged
options.D: Domestic order of $60.00 with gift wrapping -> a $3.00 gift-wrap fee is added correctly

questions.why_correct: CTFL 4.5.3: in ATDD, test cases are derived from the acceptance criteria and must cover all the characteristics of the user story without going beyond it. Gift-wrap pricing is not part of this story or its acceptance criteria. The first tests are usually positive, followed by negative tests and then non-functional characteristics.

option_notes.A: In scope - a positive test at the threshold.
option_notes.B: In scope - covers the international criterion.
option_notes.C: In scope - a negative-side test just below the threshold.
option_notes.D: Out of scope - goes beyond the user story.

questions.distractor_note: D looks thorough, but ATDD test cases must not go beyond the story's scope.
questions.alt_wording: Which test case goes beyond the scope of the user story's acceptance criteria?

questions.topic: Tests Wear Out vs Presence of Defects
questions.question: A regression suite has run unchanged for 18 months and has not found a new defect in the last 12 months, although customers keep reporting new failures. Which testing principle MOST directly suggests the corrective action the team should take?

options.A: Tests wear out
options.B: Absence-of-defects fallacy
options.C: Defects cluster together
options.D: Testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects

questions.why_correct: 'Tests wear out' (pesticide paradox): repeating the same tests makes them increasingly ineffective at detecting new defects. The prescribed remedy is to modify existing tests and test data and possibly write new tests. That is the corrective action the question asks for.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: This is about verified software still failing to meet user needs (building the wrong system), not about a stale suite.
option_notes.C: Clustering could guide where to add tests, but it does not explain why an unchanged suite stopped finding defects.
option_notes.D: True and relevant to anyone claiming the product is defect-free, but it does not tell the team what to change.

questions.distractor_note: D is plausible because the scenario hints at false confidence, but the question asks for the principle that suggests the CORRECTIVE ACTION.
questions.alt_wording: Which principle explains why repeating the same tests stops finding new defects, and what should be done?

questions.question: Experts estimate the test effort for a feature as: optimistic a = 10, most likely m = 16, pessimistic b = 34 person-hours. Using the three-point formula from CTFL, what is the estimate?

options.A: 16 +/- 4 person-hours
options.B: 18 +/- 4 person-hours
options.C: 18 +/- 24 person-hours
options.D: 20 +/- 4 person-hours

questions.why_correct: E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 = (10 + 64 + 34) / 6 = 108 / 6 = 18. SD = (b - a) / 6 = (34 - 10) / 6 = 4. So the estimate is 18 +/- 4 person-hours (between 14 and 22).

option_notes.A: Uses only the most likely value.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Uses b - a without dividing by 6 for the measurement error.
option_notes.D: 20 is the simple average (10 + 16 + 34) / 3, without the weight of 4 on m.

questions.distractor_note: D tempts anyone who forgets the 4x weighting on the most likely estimate.
questions.alt_wording: Calculate E = (a + 4m + b)/6 and SD = (b - a)/6.

questions.question:
A tester's test fails in the payment module. Consider these activities:
i. Reproducing the failure to locate where it happens
ii. Re-running the originally failing test after the fix
iii. Diagnosing the root cause and fixing it
iv. Running regression tests on the unchanged refund module after the fix

Which activities are part of DEBUGGING?

options.A: ii and iv only
options.B: i, ii and iii
options.C: i, iii and iv
options.D: i and iii only

questions.why_correct: CTFL 1.1.2: debugging is the process of finding, analyzing and removing the causes of failures - reproduction of the failure, diagnosis (finding the root cause) and fixing the cause. Confirmation testing (ii) and regression testing (iv) that follow the fix are testing activities, not debugging.

option_notes.A: Both are testing activities that follow debugging: confirmation testing and regression testing.
option_notes.B: Re-running the failing test (ii) is confirmation testing - a testing activity, even though it follows the fix.
option_notes.C: Regression testing (iv) is a testing activity, not part of debugging.
option_notes.D: Correct.

questions.distractor_note: B is the close trap: confirmation testing happens right after the fix, so it 'feels' part of debugging, but the syllabus places it under testing.
questions.alt_wording: Which tasks does the developer perform when debugging, as opposed to the tester's follow-up testing?

questions.question: Which assignment of tests to the testing quadrants is CORRECT?

options.A: Component integration tests - Q2 (business facing, support the team)
options.B: User acceptance testing - Q2 (business facing, support the team)
options.C: Usability testing - Q4 (technology facing, critique the product)
options.D: Smoke tests - Q4 (technology facing, critique the product)

questions.why_correct: CTFL 5.1.7: Q1 (technology facing, support the team) holds component and component integration tests. Q2 (business facing, support the team) holds functional tests, examples, user story tests, UX prototypes, API testing and simulations. Q3 (business facing, critique the product) holds exploratory, usability and user acceptance testing. Q4 (technology facing, critique the product) holds smoke tests and non-functional tests EXCEPT usability.

option_notes.A: Component integration tests are Q1.
option_notes.B: User acceptance testing is Q3.
option_notes.C: Usability is the explicit exception: it belongs to Q3.
option_notes.D: Correct.

questions.distractor_note: C catches candidates who remember 'non-functional = Q4' but forget the usability exception.
questions.alt_wording: Which quadrant contains smoke tests?

questions.question:
Which statements are correct?
i. In an inspection, the author may act as scribe if no one else is available.
ii. A walkthrough is led by the author.
iii. A technical review is led by a moderator.
iv. The moderator decides what is to be reviewed and provides staff and time.
v. The review leader decides who will be involved and organizes when and where the review takes place.

options.A: ii, iii and v
options.B: i, ii and iv
options.C: ii, iv and v
options.D: i, iii and v

questions.why_correct: CTFL 3.2.3/3.2.4: a walkthrough is led by the author; a technical review is led by a moderator; the review leader takes overall responsibility, deciding who is involved and when and where the review takes place. In an inspection the author cannot act as review leader or scribe. Deciding what is reviewed and providing resources is the MANAGER's responsibility.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: i and iv are false.
option_notes.C: iv is false: that is the manager's responsibility.
option_notes.D: i is false: in inspections the author cannot be the scribe or review leader.

questions.distractor_note: iv swaps the moderator (runs meetings effectively, mediation, time management, safe environment) with the manager (decides what is reviewed, provides resources).
questions.alt_wording: Which review responsibilities and leadership rules match CTFL?

questions.question: From a testing perspective, which of the following is MOST likely to be a CHALLENGE (rather than a benefit) of DevOps?

options.A: Slower feedback on code quality because every change triggers a pipeline
options.B: Manual testing from the user's perspective is no longer needed
options.C: Reduced visibility of non-functional quality characteristics
options.D: Test automation needs extra resources and may be difficult to establish and maintain

questions.why_correct: CTFL 2.1.4 lists DevOps risks and challenges: the delivery pipeline must be defined and established, CI/CD tools must be introduced and maintained, and test automation requires additional resources and may be difficult to establish and maintain. Benefits include fast feedback, shift left, automated CI/CD, and increased visibility of non-functional characteristics.

option_notes.A: Reversed: fast feedback is a key DevOps benefit.
option_notes.B: The syllabus says manual testing, especially from the user's perspective, will still be needed.
option_notes.C: Reversed: DevOps INCREASES visibility of non-functional characteristics (e.g., performance, reliability).
option_notes.D: Correct.

questions.distractor_note: C and A are benefits turned into their opposites. B is a common misconception about automation-heavy pipelines.
questions.alt_wording: What difficulty does DevOps introduce for testing?

questions.question: Which practice is NOT an example of shift left?

options.A: Performance-testing a pricing component during component testing
options.B: Running static analysis on source code before dynamic testing
options.C: Postponing security testing until system testing is finished, so that the complete system can be assessed
options.D: Using continuous integration with continuous delivery to get fast feedback

questions.why_correct: Shift left means performing testing earlier in the SDLC. CTFL 2.1.5 examples include reviewing the specification from a testing perspective, writing test cases before code, CI/CD, static analysis before dynamic testing, and non-functional testing starting at component test level where possible. Deliberately postponing security testing moves testing right, not left.

option_notes.A: Shift left: non-functional testing at component level.
option_notes.B: Shift left: static analysis before dynamic testing.
option_notes.C: NOT shift left - this is the answer.
option_notes.D: Shift left: CI/CD with fast feedback.

questions.distractor_note: A tempts readers who think performance testing belongs only at system level; the syllabus explicitly gives it as a shift-left example.
questions.alt_wording: Which option moves testing LATER in the lifecycle?

questions.question:
A state table for a door controller has 4 states (rows) and 3 events (columns). 5 cells contain valid transitions; all other cells are empty. A test suite exercises all 5 valid transitions and attempts 3 different invalid transitions, each in a separate test case.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Valid transitions coverage is 100% and all transitions coverage is 100%, because attempting invalid transitions is optional.
options.B: Valid transitions coverage is 100% and all transitions coverage is 37.5%.
options.C: Valid transitions coverage is 62.5% and all transitions coverage is about 66.7%.
options.D: Valid transitions coverage is 100% and all transitions coverage is about 66.7%.

questions.why_correct: In all transitions coverage, the coverage items are all transitions in the state table: 4 x 3 = 12 cells (5 valid + 7 invalid). Exercised or attempted: 5 + 3 = 8. Coverage = 8/12 = about 66.7%. Valid transitions coverage = 5/5 = 100%. Testing one invalid transition per test case avoids defect masking.

option_notes.A: All transitions coverage requires ALSO attempting the invalid transitions; 4 of the 7 were not attempted.
option_notes.B: 37.5% = 3/8 - wrongly divides the invalid transitions attempted by the transitions exercised.
option_notes.C: Valid transitions coverage is 5/5, not 5/8.
option_notes.D: Correct.

questions.distractor_note: Count the denominator from the state table (states x events), not from the diagram.
questions.alt_wording: How do valid transitions coverage and all transitions coverage differ in their coverage items?

questions.topic: Test Analysis vs Test Design Tasks
questions.question: Which task belongs to TEST ANALYSIS rather than test design?

options.A: Evaluating the test basis and test object to identify defects and assess testability
options.B: Identifying coverage items that guide the test case inputs
options.C: Defining test data requirements and designing the test environment
options.D: Elaborating test conditions into test charters

questions.why_correct: CTFL 1.4.1: test analysis analyzes the test basis to identify testable features, defines and prioritizes test conditions, and evaluates the test basis and test object to identify defects and assess testability ('what to test'). Coverage items, test data requirements, test environment design and test charters belong to test design ('how to test').

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Test design: identifying coverage items.
option_notes.C: Test design: test data requirements and test environment design.
option_notes.D: Test design: test conditions are elaborated into test cases and other testware such as test charters.

questions.distractor_note: D is the trap: test charters feel 'analytical' because they hold objectives, but the syllabus lists them as a test design work product.
questions.alt_wording: Which activity answers 'what to test?' and includes evaluating testability?

questions.question:
A risk register uses risk level = likelihood x impact (likelihood 0-1, impact 1-10):
R1: Third-party payment SDK delivered late - L 0.8, I 5
R2: Incorrect currency rounding on invoices - L 0.5, I 6
R3: Checkout response time above 5 s at peak load - L 0.6, I 4
R4: Testers lack security testing skills - L 0.9, I 4

Which PRODUCT risk has the highest risk level?

options.A: R1
options.B: R2
options.C: R3
options.D: R4

questions.why_correct: Levels: R1 = 4.0, R2 = 3.0, R3 = 2.4, R4 = 3.6. R1 (supplier delivery) and R4 (people skills) are PROJECT risks. The product risks are R2 (incorrect calculation) and R3 (inadequate response time); R2 has the higher level.

option_notes.A: Highest overall, but a project risk (supplier issue).
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: A product risk, but its level (2.4) is lower than R2's.
option_notes.D: A project risk (people issue).

questions.distractor_note: Calculate first, then filter: the two highest scores are both project risks.
questions.alt_wording: Among quality-related risks, which has the greatest likelihood x impact?

questions.topic: Contingency Plan vs Other Risk Responses
questions.question: For the product risk 'interest is miscalculated after the overnight batch', which response is a CONTINGENCY PLAN?

options.A: Deciding to live with the risk because it affects only a handful of dormant accounts
options.B: Moving the financial liability to the batch vendor through the contract
options.C: Preparing a rollback procedure and a manual calculation fallback to use if the failure happens after release
options.D: Assigning more independent testers with banking domain skills to the batch tests

questions.why_correct: CTFL 5.2.4 lists response options to analyzed product risks: risk mitigation by testing, risk acceptance, risk transfer, and a contingency plan. A contingency plan defines what will be done IF the risk occurs - here, a rollback and a manual fallback.

option_notes.A: Risk acceptance.
option_notes.B: Risk transfer.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Risk mitigation by testing (right skills, appropriate independence).

questions.distractor_note: D is the most 'testing-like' answer, but mitigation reduces the risk level beforehand; a contingency plan deals with the consequences after the risk occurs.
questions.alt_wording: Which response prepares for the risk occurring rather than reducing it?

questions.question: A test suite achieves 100% statement coverage of a function that contains the statement 'ratio = total / count'. Which conclusion is BEST?

options.A: Branch coverage of the function is therefore also 100%.
options.B: Any defect located in the division statement would have caused a failure and been detected.
options.C: All the decision logic in the function has been tested.
options.D: Every executable statement was executed at least once, but a division-by-zero defect may still go undetected because it depends on the data used.

questions.why_correct: CTFL 4.3.1: 100% statement coverage ensures every executable statement has been exercised at least once. It does not ensure that all decision logic has been tested, and a defect is not necessarily revealed by executing it - some defects show up only with specific data (here, count = 0).

option_notes.A: Statement coverage does not imply branch coverage; branch coverage subsumes statement coverage, not the other way round.
option_notes.B: Executing a defective statement does not guarantee a failure; it depends on the data.
option_notes.C: Statement coverage can miss decision outcomes that contain no statements, such as an empty else branch.
option_notes.D: Correct.

questions.distractor_note: A reverses the subsumption relationship - a frequent exam trap.
questions.alt_wording: What does 100% statement coverage guarantee, and what does it NOT guarantee?

questions.question: A loyalty discount applies to order amounts from 100.00 to 499.99 (amounts have exactly two decimal places). Which MINIMAL set of test values achieves 100% 2-value BVA coverage for the boundaries of the discount partition?
questions.why_correct: The partitions are <100.00, 100.00-499.99, and >=500.00. The smallest increment is 0.01, so the boundary values are 99.99 / 100.00 at the lower boundary and 499.99 / 500.00 at the upper boundary. 2-value BVA covers each boundary value and its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition, giving these 4 values.

option_notes.A: Ignores the 0.01 precision; 499 is not a boundary value and 499.00-499.99 is still in the valid partition.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: This is a 3-value BVA set, not a minimal 2-value set.
option_notes.D: Only covers the valid side of each boundary.

questions.distractor_note: A tempts candidates who treat the input as an integer. Always check the precision of the input first.
questions.alt_wording: What are the boundary values when the smallest increment is 0.01?

questions.question:
An insurance quote accepts an integer age. Rules: below 18 rejected; 18-25 high premium; 26-64 standard premium; 65-99 senior premium; above 99 rejected. Consider only integer inputs.

Tests use ages 17, 25, 26, 64 and 100. What equivalence partitioning coverage is achieved?
questions.why_correct: There are 5 partitions: <18 (invalid), 18-25, 26-64, 65-99, >99 (invalid). Age 17 covers <18; 25 covers 18-25; 26 and 64 both cover 26-64; 100 covers >99. The 65-99 partition is not covered. Coverage = 4/5 = 80%.

option_notes.A: Miscounts the number of partitions.
option_notes.B: This would be 3/5 - one too few partitions counted as covered.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: 65-99 is never exercised; 26 and 64 are in the same partition.

questions.distractor_note: Values that look like 'different' boundaries (26 and 64) still sit in the same partition and count only once for EP.
questions.alt_wording: How many partitions do these test values exercise, as a percentage of all partitions?

questions.topic: Minimum Tests for Statement vs Branch Coverage
questions.question:
Consider this pseudocode:

1  read amount, isVip
2  discount = 0
3  if amount > 100 then
4      discount = 10
5  endif
6  if isVip then
7      discount = discount + 5
8  else
9      log "standard"
10 endif
11 print discount

What is the MINIMUM number of test cases to achieve 100% statement coverage and 100% branch coverage, respectively?

options.A: 1 and 2
options.B: 2 and 2
options.C: 2 and 4
options.D: 3 and 4

questions.why_correct: Statement coverage: line 4 needs amount > 100, line 7 needs isVip = true, and line 9 needs isVip = false. One test cannot have isVip both true and false, so 2 tests are needed (e.g., 150/true and any/false). Branch coverage needs both outcomes of each decision: (amount > 100 T, isVip T) and (amount > 100 F, isVip F) cover all four outcomes in 2 tests, e.g., (150, true) and (50, false).

option_notes.A: The else-branch statement on line 9 forces a second test for statement coverage.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: 4 is the number of decision outcomes, but two tests can each cover one outcome of both decisions.
option_notes.D: Overcounts both.

questions.distractor_note: The if-then-else on isVip contains a statement in EACH branch, so statement coverage already needs 2 tests. Branch coverage does not need 4, because the two independent decisions can be combined.
questions.alt_wording: How many tests are needed to execute every statement, and how many to take every decision outcome?

questions.question:
Which statements describe good testing practices that apply regardless of the SDLC?
i. All test levels should share the same objectives to avoid gaps between levels.
ii. Test analysis and design for a test level begin during the corresponding development phase.
iii. Testers review work products as soon as drafts are available.
iv. Test activities are needed only for development activities that produce executable code.

options.A: i and iv
options.B: i and ii
options.C: ii and iii
options.D: iii and iv

questions.why_correct: CTFL 2.1.2: for every development activity there is a corresponding test activity; different test levels have specific and DIFFERENT test objectives (to avoid redundancy while staying comprehensive); test analysis and design for a level begin during the corresponding development phase; testers are involved in reviewing work products as soon as drafts are available.

option_notes.A: Both statements contradict the syllabus.
option_notes.B: i is wrong: levels need different objectives.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: iv is wrong: every development activity (including requirements and design) has a corresponding test activity.

questions.distractor_note: Statement i sounds reasonable ('avoid gaps') but reverses the actual practice of having distinct objectives per level.
questions.alt_wording: Which practices hold for sequential, iterative and incremental models alike?

questions.question: A team uses containerization to spin up identical, disposable test environments on demand for each test run. In the CTFL classification of test tools, which category does this BEST fit?

options.A: Non-functional testing tools
options.B: Tools supporting scalability and deployment standardization
options.C: DevOps tools
options.D: Test design and implementation tools

questions.why_correct: CTFL 6.1 lists tools supporting scalability and deployment standardization (e.g., virtual machines, containerization tools) as a separate category. DevOps tools support the DevOps delivery pipeline, workflow tracking, automated build processes and CI/CD. Test design and implementation tools generate test cases, test data and test procedures. Non-functional testing tools support non-functional testing that is difficult or impossible to do manually.

option_notes.A: These support, for example, performance or load testing.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Close, because containers are often used inside pipelines, but CTFL names containerization explicitly under scalability and deployment standardization.
option_notes.D: These generate test cases, test data and test procedures, not environments.

questions.distractor_note: C is the deliberate near-miss: a pipeline may use containers, but the category is decided by what the tool itself provides.
questions.alt_wording: Which tool category includes virtual machines and containerization tools?

questions.question:
Consider this pseudocode:

1  if score >= 90 then
2      grade = "A"
3  else if score >= 75 then
4      grade = "B"
5  else
6      grade = "C"
7  endif

Tests use score = 95 and score = 80. Counting the decision outcomes (conditional branches) only, which statement is correct?

options.A: Branch coverage is 100%, because both grade A and grade B paths were executed.
options.B: Branch coverage is 50%, because only two of the three grades were produced.
options.C: Branch coverage is about 66.7%; adding a test with score = 60 gives 100%.
options.D: Branch coverage is 75%; adding a test with score = 60 gives 100%.

questions.why_correct: There are 2 decisions with 2 outcomes each = 4 conditional branches. Score 95: first decision TRUE. Score 80: first decision FALSE, second decision TRUE. The second decision's FALSE outcome (leading to grade C) is not taken. Coverage = 3/4 = 75%. A score below 75 (e.g., 60) takes the missing outcome.

option_notes.A: The FALSE outcome of 'score >= 75' was never taken.
option_notes.B: Counts grades instead of decision outcomes.
option_notes.C: Treats the three grade paths as the coverage items (2/3) instead of the 4 decision outcomes.
option_notes.D: Correct.

questions.distractor_note: C mixes path or grade counting with branch counting. Branch coverage counts decision OUTCOMES.
questions.alt_wording: How many of the four decision outcomes are exercised by these two tests?

questions.topic: Test Management Role vs Testing Role
questions.question: In an Agile team, the development manager defines the test approach for the release, tracks test progress and decides when testing of the iteration can be completed. Team members analyze, design and execute the tests. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: In Agile development, the test management role must be performed by a test manager outside the team.
options.B: This set-up is invalid because one person cannot perform both test management and development management tasks.
options.C: The development manager is performing the test management role; the role is defined by its tasks, not by a job title.
options.D: There is no test management role in this team, because nobody holds the job title of test manager.

questions.why_correct: CTFL 1.4.5: the test management role (mainly test planning, monitoring, control and completion) can be performed by a team leader, a test manager, a development manager, etc. In Agile some test management tasks may be handled by the team, and tasks spanning multiple teams may be done by test managers outside the team.

option_notes.A: Only tasks spanning multiple teams or the whole organization MAY be done outside the team - it is not a 'must'.
option_notes.B: The syllabus explicitly allows one person to take on more than one role.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Roles are about responsibilities, not job titles.

questions.distractor_note: A distorts a real sentence from the syllabus by turning 'may, for cross-team tasks' into 'must'.
questions.alt_wording: Who can carry out test planning, monitoring, control and completion?

questions.question: Which pairing of a user story 'C' with its meaning is CORRECT?

options.A: Card - the medium describing a user story, such as an index card or an entry in an electronic board
options.B: Conversation - the acceptance criteria
options.C: Confirmation - explains how the software will be used; it can be documented or verbal
options.D: Card - the acceptance criteria

questions.why_correct: CTFL 4.5.1: Card is the medium describing a user story (an index card, an entry in an electronic board). Conversation explains how the software will be used (it can be documented or verbal). Confirmation is the acceptance criteria.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Acceptance criteria are the CONFIRMATION.
option_notes.C: That describes CONVERSATION.
option_notes.D: Acceptance criteria are the CONFIRMATION, not the card.

questions.distractor_note: B and C swap Conversation and Confirmation - the most common mix-up.
questions.alt_wording: Match card, conversation and confirmation to their meanings.

questions.topic: Progress Report vs Completion Report Content
questions.question: Which item is typically included in a test PROGRESS report but NOT in a test COMPLETION report?

options.A: Test metrics
options.B: Lessons learned relevant to the testing
options.C: Testing planned for the next period
options.D: Testing impediments and their workarounds

questions.why_correct: CTFL 5.3.2: progress reports include the testing period, test progress, impediments and workarounds, test metrics, new and changed risks, and testing planned for the next period. Completion reports include a test summary, an evaluation against the plan, deviations, impediments and workarounds, metrics, unmitigated risks and unfixed defects, and lessons learned. Only 'testing planned for the next period' is unique to progress reports.

option_notes.A: Appears in both (completion metrics are based on progress reports).
option_notes.B: Belongs to the completion report only - the reverse direction.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Appears in both report types.

questions.distractor_note: B is the reverse trap: it is unique to one report, but to the COMPLETION report.
questions.alt_wording: Which content looks forward to the next reporting period?

questions.question: A team replaces its detailed test scripts with a high-level checklist for regression checks of a mobile banking app. What is the MOST likely effect?

options.A: Less coverage, but greater repeatability
options.B: No change in repeatability, because the checklist items are fixed
options.C: The checklist stays effective indefinitely, because its items come from experience
options.D: Potentially greater coverage, but less repeatability

questions.why_correct: CTFL 4.4.3: when detailed test cases are absent, checklist-based testing gives guidelines and some consistency. Because checklists are high-level, testing is likely to vary in practice, which can give greater coverage but less repeatability. Checklists also need regular updates, because developers learn to avoid the same errors and the items lose effectiveness.

option_notes.A: Reversed.
option_notes.B: High-level items are carried out differently each time, so repeatability drops.
option_notes.C: Checklists lose effectiveness over time and must be updated regularly.
option_notes.D: Correct.

questions.distractor_note: A is the mirror-image trap. Remember: high-level means more variability, which means more coverage and less repeatability.
questions.alt_wording: What trade-off comes with using high-level checklists instead of detailed test cases?

questions.question:
A password must be 8 to 64 characters long (integer lengths). Tests use lengths 7, 8, 9, 64 and 65.

What 3-value boundary value analysis coverage is achieved?
questions.why_correct: The boundary values are 7 and 8 (lower boundary) and 64 and 65 (upper boundary). In 3-value BVA each boundary value has three coverage items: itself and both neighbours. Unique items: 6, 7, 8, 9 and 63, 64, 65, 66 = 8 items. Tests cover 7, 8, 9, 64, 65 = 5 items. Coverage = 5/8 = 62.5%.

option_notes.A: Results from counting 10 items or covering only 4.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Results from wrongly counting only 6 items (e.g., 7, 8, 9 and 63, 64, 65).
option_notes.D: This is the 2-value BVA result (7, 8, 64, 65 all covered); 3-value BVA needs more.

questions.distractor_note: D is the strongest trap: the set achieves 100% 2-value BVA, so a candidate who ignores 'three-value' picks it.
questions.alt_wording: Using the three-value variant, what fraction of the coverage items do these lengths exercise?

questions.question: Which statement about the whole team approach is NOT correct?

options.A: Testers help business representatives create suitable acceptance tests and agree on test automation approaches with developers.
options.B: Any team member with the necessary knowledge and skills can perform any task, and everyone is responsible for quality.
options.C: Team members share the same workspace, physical or virtual, because co-location helps communication.
options.D: Because everyone is responsible for quality, it remains the preferred option even where a high level of test independence is required, for example in safety-critical systems.

questions.why_correct: CTFL 1.5.2 states that, depending on the context, the whole team approach may not always be appropriate. In some situations, such as safety-critical ones, a high level of test independence may be needed instead. The other three statements come straight from the syllabus.

option_notes.A: Correct description of how testers work in the whole team approach.
option_notes.B: Correct statement of the whole team approach.
option_notes.C: Correct; the workspace can be physical or virtual.
option_notes.D: NOT correct - this is the answer.

questions.distractor_note: D starts with a true premise ('everyone is responsible for quality') and ends with a false conclusion. Read the whole statement.
questions.alt_wording: In which situation might the whole team approach be inappropriate?

questions.question: A defect in the coupon calculation is fixed. The original failing test case is obsolete because the coupon screen was redesigned, so the tester writes a NEW test case covering the changed code needed for the fix and runs it. How is this test BEST classified?

options.A: Component integration testing, because the fix touched a redesigned screen
options.B: Regression testing, because it is a newly written test case
options.C: Confirmation testing, because it checks that the original defect has been fixed
options.D: Regression testing, because it does not re-run the test that originally failed

questions.why_correct: CTFL 2.2.3: confirmation testing confirms that an original defect has been successfully fixed. It may re-run all test cases that failed because of the defect, or it may also add NEW tests to cover changes needed to fix the defect. Regression testing checks that a change has not caused adverse consequences, including in unchanged parts.

option_notes.A: A test level is not the classification asked for, and nothing here concerns component interfaces.
option_notes.B: Being new does not make a test a regression test; what matters is its purpose.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Confirmation testing does not require re-running the exact failing test.

questions.distractor_note: The trap is to classify by HOW the test was created (new vs re-run) instead of by its PURPOSE (checking the fix vs checking for side effects).
questions.alt_wording: Is a newly written test that checks a fix a confirmation test or a regression test?

questions.question: Which statement BEST contrasts static testing and dynamic testing?

options.A: Static testing can be applied to non-executable work products and can measure characteristics such as maintainability that do not depend on executing code; dynamic testing is needed for characteristics such as performance efficiency.
options.B: Because static testing finds defects earlier and cheaper, it can replace dynamic testing for most quality characteristics.
options.C: Dynamic testing is more effective than static testing at detecting unreachable code.
options.D: Static testing finds failures directly, while dynamic testing finds defects directly.

questions.why_correct: CTFL 3.1.3: static testing finds defects directly, while dynamic testing causes failures from which the defects are found by analysis. Static testing can be applied to non-executable work products and can measure quality characteristics that do not depend on executing code (e.g., maintainability), while dynamic testing is needed for those that do (e.g., performance efficiency). The two approaches complement each other.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: They complement each other; neither replaces the other.
option_notes.C: Unreachable code is a typical defect found by STATIC testing (e.g., static analysis).
option_notes.D: Reversed: static testing finds DEFECTS directly; dynamic testing causes FAILURES.

questions.distractor_note: D is the classic swap trap. Static testing finds defects, dynamic testing reveals failures.
questions.alt_wording: How do static testing and dynamic testing differ in what they can evaluate?

questions.topic: Valid Transitions Coverage With a Final State
questions.question:
A subscription has states Trial, Active, Suspended and Cancelled. Cancelled is a final state (no outgoing transitions). The valid transitions are:
- Trial --pay--> Active
- Trial --cancel--> Cancelled
- Active --paymentFails--> Suspended
- Suspended --pay--> Active
- Suspended --cancel--> Cancelled
- Active --cancel--> Cancelled

Every test case starts in Trial. What is the MINIMUM number of test cases needed for 100% valid transitions (0-switch) coverage?
questions.why_correct:
Three different transitions enter the final state Cancelled (from Trial, Active and Suspended). Once a test case reaches Cancelled it cannot continue, so each test case can cover at most one of these three transitions. That means at least 3 test cases, and 3 are enough:
T1: Trial -cancel-> Cancelled
T2: Trial -pay-> Active -paymentFails-> Suspended -pay-> Active -cancel-> Cancelled
T3: Trial -pay-> Active -paymentFails-> Suspended -cancel-> Cancelled

option_notes.A: One path cannot use more than one transition into the final state.
option_notes.B: Two test cases still leave one of the three transitions into Cancelled uncovered.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: 6 is the number of coverage items (valid transitions), not the minimum number of test cases.

questions.distractor_note: The decisive clue is the final state: count the transitions INTO a state with no exit. Each one needs its own test case.
questions.alt_wording: How many test sequences are needed to exercise every valid transition when a final state ends each sequence?

questions.topic: Severity vs Priority in a Defect Report
questions.question: The day before a major brand launch, a tester finds that the company name is misspelled on the login page. The defect report states 'Severity: Low, Priority: Critical'. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: The report is valid; severity is the degree of impact on stakeholders or requirements, while priority is the urgency to fix.
options.B: Priority should be lowered to match the low severity, because priority is derived from severity.
options.C: Severity should be raised to Critical, because the business wants it fixed quickly.
options.D: The report is inconsistent; severity and priority must have the same level.

questions.why_correct: CTFL 5.5 lists severity (degree of impact on the interests of stakeholders or requirements) and priority to fix as separate defect report fields. A cosmetic typo has low functional impact but may be very urgent for business reasons (the brand launch), so low severity with high priority is a valid combination.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Priority is not derived from severity.
option_notes.C: Urgency affects priority, not severity.
option_notes.D: They are independent attributes.

questions.distractor_note: B and C both assume one attribute drives the other. Severity and priority answer different questions: impact vs urgency.
questions.alt_wording: How do defect severity and defect priority differ?

questions.question: A bank is retiring its legacy loan system. Loan records must be kept for ten years after retirement. Which testing is MOST appropriate for this maintenance trigger?

options.A: Full regression testing of all loan functions before shutdown
options.B: Testing data conversion in the target system, since retirement is a form of migration
options.C: Testing data archiving, and testing the restore and retrieval procedures after archiving
options.D: No testing, because a retired system no longer delivers business value

questions.why_correct: CTFL 2.3.1 lists retirement as a maintenance trigger: when an application reaches end of life, data archiving may need to be tested if long data retention periods are required, and testing restore and retrieval procedures after archiving may also be needed.

option_notes.A: Regression testing of functions that are being switched off adds little value.
option_notes.B: Data conversion testing belongs to the 'upgrades or migrations' trigger, when data is migrated INTO the system being maintained.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Retirement can still require testing, especially when data must be retained.

questions.distractor_note: B confuses two different triggers: migration (data moved into a maintained system) vs retirement (data archived from a system that is being switched off).
questions.alt_wording: What should be tested when an application reaches end of life and its data must be retained?

questions.question: In a review meeting, participants go through each logged anomaly and decide its status, owner and required actions. They also judge the quality level of the requirements document and agree that a follow-up review is needed. Which review activity is this?

options.A: Communication and analysis
options.B: Fixing and reporting
options.C: Review initiation
options.D: Individual review

questions.why_correct: CTFL 3.2.2: in communication and analysis, the anomalies (which are not necessarily defects) are analyzed and discussed, and for each one a decision is made on its status, ownership and required actions. This is typically done in a review meeting, where participants also decide the quality level of the work product and the follow-up actions, which may include a follow-up review.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Fixing and reporting creates defect reports, follows up corrective actions, and accepts the work product once the exit criteria are met.
option_notes.C: Review initiation ensures everyone has access to the work product and understands their role.
option_notes.D: Individual review is where each reviewer finds and logs anomalies on their own.

questions.distractor_note: B is the close neighbour: 'follow-up' sounds like fixing and reporting, but DECIDING the follow-up actions happens in communication and analysis.
questions.alt_wording: In which review activity are anomaly status, ownership and actions decided?
